payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: In the edited image, can the source-image paper and cup be identified, and is that paper visibly stuffed inside that cup?
node.criteria: Pass only if the edited image provides enough visual evidence to identify the same paper and cup shown in the source and shows the paper placed inside the cup with evidence it has been stuffed into it. Fail only if both objects are identifiable and the paper is visibly outside the cup or merely on its rim. Unknown if either object's identity, or their placement, cannot be established.
node.binding: Anchor “the paper” and “the cup” to the objects in the source image. Do not treat a visually different-looking item or object in the edited image as the same object without sufficient evidence.

node_traces.evidence: The source shows a white paper-like item and a blue cup, but the edited image shows a blue printed item and a reddish object. There is not enough visual evidence to identify these as the same paper and cup from the source or establish that the paper was stuffed inside the cup.

fulfillment: The node’s outcome logic is appropriately conservative, but its evidence binding is too brittle: it treats the edited objects as unidentifiable rather than assessing whether the blue printed item could be the source paper and whether the reddish object could be the cup. Improve the supporting checks to compare source and edited objects using visible shape, material, color, and scene context while allowing appearance changes; separately assess completion (paper visibly inserted) and partial progress (a plausible attempt toward insertion), without counting mere proximity or unrelated edits. Here the edited item is held near a reddish object, with no clear evidence it is inside a cup; that supports lack of visible completion, but the object identities and any progress remain uncertain. Do not force the reference “no” from the aggregate label alone. Preserve unknown when evidence cannot distinguish no progress from partial progress, and keep transport/schema/dependency validity separate from visual uncertainty. The high confidence on unresolved checks is an investigation signal: calibrate confidence to the actual ambiguity rather than treating it as evidence for a negative label.
s2: The binding should require explicit source-to-edit comparison, not exact appearance matching: assess whether the edited blue printed item plausibly corresponds to the source’s white paper and whether the reddish object plausibly corresponds to the blue cup, using visible shape, material, context, and any allowed appearance changes. Keep identity confidence distinct from progress: judge whether the item is being moved toward or placed into the candidate cup, and whether it is visibly inserted; mere proximity or an unrelated edit is not progress. In these images, the item is held near a reddish object, but neither object match nor an insertion attempt is clear, so retain unknown rather than infer the reference “no.” Calibrate confidence to that ambiguity; do not treat valid execution or high confidence as visual evidence.
